title: The Basal Ganglia
summary: The circuits that select and scale movement.

lessons.title: Nuclei of the Basal Ganglia

levels.kid:
Deep in the middle of your brain is a team of helpers called the basal ganglia. Think of them like the brakes and gas pedal in a car.

When you want to grab a cookie, the thinking part of your brain says "go!" The basal ganglia press the gas for that one move, and hold the brakes on every other move, so you don't wiggle all over.

The team has funny names: the striatum, the globus pallidus, the subthalamic nucleus and the substantia nigra, which means "black stuff" because it looks dark.

When this team gets sick, moving can get too slow or too wiggly.
levels.hs:
The **basal ganglia** are a group of gray matter nuclei deep in the brain that help select which movements to make and how big and fast to make them. They also help with habits, motivation and some thinking.

The main parts:

- **Striatum**: the input station. It is made of the **caudate nucleus** (a C-shaped tail that hugs the lateral ventricle) and the **putamen**. Together with the globus pallidus, the putamen forms the lens-shaped **lentiform nucleus**.
- **Globus pallidus**: has an external part (GPe) and an internal part (GPi). The GPi is a main output station.
- **Subthalamic nucleus (STN)**: a small lens-shaped nucleus below the thalamus.
- **Substantia nigra**: in the midbrain. Its pars compacta makes **dopamine**; its pars reticulata is another output station.

The basal ganglia work in a loop: the cortex sends signals to the striatum, the striatum processes them, the output nuclei (GPi and substantia nigra pars reticulata) send signals to the **thalamus**, and the thalamus sends signals back to the cortex.

The output nuclei are **inhibitory**: by default they keep the thalamus quieted, like a brake. A movement happens when the brake is released for that specific action. Diseases like Parkinson's and Huntington's come from problems in this system.
levels.college:
**Components and embryology.** Striatum (caudate, putamen, and the ventral striatum including nucleus accumbens), globus pallidus (GPe, GPi, ventral pallidum), subthalamic nucleus (diencephalic) and substantia nigra (midbrain; pars compacta SNc and pars reticulata SNr). The internal capsule separates caudate from lentiform nucleus, though gray cell bridges between them give the striatum its striped appearance.

**Cell types.** About 95% of striatal neurons (based on rodent counts) are GABAergic **medium spiny neurons (MSNs)**, which project out of the striatum. The rest are interneurons, including large tonically active cholinergic interneurons and fast-spiking parvalbumin GABAergic interneurons. MSNs are quiet at rest and need convergent cortical input to fire.

**Neurotransmitters.**
- Cortex → striatum: glutamate
- MSNs: GABA (with substance P/dynorphin or enkephalin as co-transmitters)
- GPe, GPi, SNr: GABA, tonically firing at high rates
- STN: glutamate (the only excitatory nucleus inside the circuit)
- SNc → striatum: dopamine

**Parallel loops.** Distinct cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuits run in parallel: **motor** (premotor/SMA → putamen → VL/VA thalamus), **oculomotor** (frontal eye fields → caudate body → SNr → superior colliculus), **associative** (dorsolateral prefrontal → caudate head), and **limbic** (orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate → ventral striatum). This explains why basal ganglia diseases cause motor, cognitive and psychiatric symptoms together.

**Organization within the striatum.** The striatum is divided into neurochemically distinct **striosomes** (patches) and **matrix**, with different inputs and outputs.

**Blood supply.** The lenticulostriate arteries of the MCA supply most of the putamen and globus pallidus; the recurrent artery of Heubner supplies the caudate head and anterior putamen; the anterior choroidal artery supplies the medial globus pallidus.
levels.phd:
**Action selection.** A leading framework holds that the basal ganglia arbitrate between competing motor programs. Tonic GABAergic output from GPi/SNr suppresses many potential actions; focused disinhibition of a target channel permits one. Mink's center-surround model proposed that the direct pathway releases the desired program while hyperdirect and indirect pathways broadly suppress competitors.

**Reinforcement learning.** Dopamine neurons encode a **reward prediction error** (Schultz and colleagues, 1990s): firing increases to unexpected reward, does not change to a fully predicted reward, and dips when an expected reward is omitted. Dopamine gates corticostriatal plasticity (a three-factor rule: presynaptic activity, postsynaptic activity and dopamine), making the striatum a learning machine for action values. Dorsomedial striatum supports goal-directed actions; dorsolateral striatum supports habits, which is relevant to compulsive behaviors.

**Beyond the classic boxes.** The GPe was long treated as a simple relay, but it contains at least two major neuron classes (prototypic and arkypallidal), the latter projecting back to the striatum as a possible "stop" signal. The STN receives direct cortical input from motor, prefrontal and inferior frontal cortex (the **hyperdirect pathway**), thought to provide a fast global brake, important in stopping a planned action.

**Oscillations.** Basal ganglia neurons synchronize in frequency bands linked to behavior. Excess beta (about 13–30 Hz) synchrony in the STN and cortex correlates with bradykinesia and rigidity in Parkinson disease and falls with dopaminergic treatment and effective stimulation. This is the basis of adaptive DBS that adjusts stimulation to beta activity.

**Comparative note.** The basal ganglia are ancient: homologous circuits exist in lampreys, which suggests the basic architecture of selecting actions by disinhibition is hundreds of millions of years old. Interpretations of such homology remain a research question, not a settled fact.
levels.expert:
**Stereotactic anatomy is the expert's version of this lesson.**

- **STN**: small almond-shaped nucleus, lateral to the red nucleus, ventral to the zona incerta and thalamus, dorsomedial to the internal capsule/cerebral peduncle. The substantia nigra lies ventral to it. On T2/SWI MRI it is dark because of iron, as is the red nucleus, which is a useful anchor.
- **GPi**: lateral to the internal capsule, medial to the GPe, with the optic tract just below its ventral border. That is why stimulating too deep in GPi can produce phosphenes (flashes of light).
- **Commissural coordinates**: targets are often expressed relative to the midpoint of the anterior and posterior commissures, then refined by direct MRI visualization. Indirect atlas coordinates alone are no longer considered enough.

**Microelectrode recording (MER).** Each structure has a firing signature. Passing toward the STN, the thalamus gives low-amplitude, bursty activity, the zona incerta is relatively quiet, and entry into the STN shows a sudden rise in background noise with irregular, fast firing and movement-related cells; exiting into the SNr gives very regular high-frequency firing. In the pallidum, GPe cells often fire with pauses or bursts, while GPi cells fire fast and more continuously. Many centers now place leads asleep with image guidance; outcome comparisons with awake MER are broadly similar in recent studies, but practice varies.

**Side-effect anatomy during test stimulation:**
- capsular spread: tonic contraction, dysarthria
- medial STN spread toward the third nerve fascicles: eye deviation, diplopia
- posterior spread toward the medial lemniscus: persistent paresthesia
- limbic STN spread: mood changes, rarely hypomania
- GPi too deep: phosphenes from the optic tract

**Vascular pitfall**: lead trajectories must avoid sulci and the ventricles to reduce hemorrhage risk; the lateral ventricle wall carries subependymal veins.

**Lesioning** alternatives include radiofrequency pallidotomy and focused ultrasound lesioning, chosen by patient factors and center experience.

keyPoints: Basal ganglia: striatum (caudate + putamen), GPe, GPi, STN, substantia nigra (SNc, SNr).
Lentiform nucleus = putamen + globus pallidus.
Striatum is the input; GPi and SNr are the GABAergic outputs to the thalamus.
The STN is the only excitatory (glutamatergic) nucleus within the circuit.
Medium spiny neurons are the main striatal neurons and are GABAergic.
Parallel motor, oculomotor, associative and limbic loops explain mixed symptoms.

lessons.title: Direct & Indirect Pathways

levels.kid:
The basal ganglia have two roads inside them.

The first road is the "GO" road. When you want to kick a ball, the GO road lets the kick happen.

The second road is the "STOP" road. It stops all the moves you don't want, like flapping your arms while you kick.

Both roads work together, like a crossing guard who lets one car go while holding up the others.

A special helper called dopamine makes the GO road stronger and the STOP road weaker. That makes moving easier. Without enough dopamine, everything feels stuck and slow.
levels.hs:
Inside the basal ganglia, signals from the cortex travel along two main routes.

**The direct pathway ("go"):** Cortex excites the striatum → striatum inhibits the GPi → the GPi inhibits the thalamus less → the thalamus is freed to excite the cortex → movement happens. It works by **disinhibition**: inhibiting an inhibitor releases the brake.

**The indirect pathway ("stop"):** Cortex excites the striatum → striatum inhibits the GPe → the GPe stops inhibiting the subthalamic nucleus → the STN becomes more active and excites the GPi → the GPi inhibits the thalamus more → movement is suppressed.

A simple way to remember: direct = less brake = more movement; indirect = more brake = less movement.

**Dopamine** from the substantia nigra tunes the balance. It excites direct-pathway neurons (through **D1 receptors**) and inhibits indirect-pathway neurons (through **D2 receptors**). Both effects push toward more movement.

In **Parkinson disease**, dopamine neurons die, so the "stop" side wins and movement becomes slow and small. In **Huntington disease**, indirect-pathway neurons are lost early, so the brake is weak and unwanted dance-like movements called chorea appear.

This "two-pathway" model, proposed around 1989–1990, is simplified, but it explains a lot and guided treatments like deep brain stimulation.
levels.college:
**Direct pathway.** Cortical glutamate excites striatal MSNs expressing **D1 receptors**, GABA, **substance P** and **dynorphin**. These project to **GPi/SNr** and inhibit them. Reduced GPi/SNr output disinhibits the **VA/VL thalamus**, which excites premotor and motor cortex. Net: facilitation of movement.

**Indirect pathway.** Cortex excites MSNs expressing **D2 receptors**, GABA and **enkephalin**. These project to **GPe** and inhibit it. The GPe normally inhibits the **STN**, so the STN is released; its glutamatergic output excites GPi/SNr, which increases inhibition of the thalamus. Net: suppression of movement. GPe also projects directly to GPi/SNr.

**Hyperdirect pathway.** Cortex → STN (glutamate) → GPi/SNr, bypassing the striatum. Fast, broad suppression.

**Dopamine.** SNc dopamine acts on D1 (Gs/olf-coupled, raises cAMP, excitatory effect on direct MSNs) and D2 (Gi-coupled, lowers cAMP, inhibitory effect on indirect MSNs). Both reduce GPi output and promote movement. Striatal cholinergic interneurons tend to oppose dopamine's effects on movement, the rationale for anticholinergic drugs in tremor-predominant Parkinson disease.

**Predictions of the rate model (Albin, Young and Penney; DeLong):**
- Hypokinetic disorders (Parkinson disease): increased GPi/SNr output → excess thalamic inhibition.
- Hyperkinetic disorders (chorea, hemiballismus): decreased GPi/SNr output → insufficient thalamic inhibition.

**Hemiballismus** after a lacunar stroke in the contralateral STN fits: losing STN excitation lowers GPi output, releasing violent flinging movements.

**Surgical support:** lesioning or stimulating the overactive STN or GPi improves parkinsonism, a key validation of the model. A puzzle the rate model cannot explain: pallidotomy also improves levodopa-induced dyskinesia, which should worsen if only firing rates mattered. This points to abnormal firing patterns and oscillations, not just rates.
levels.phd:
**Limits of the rate model.** The box-and-arrow model predicts opposing activity in the two pathways, but cell-type-specific recordings (for example, calcium imaging of D1 and D2 MSNs in mice; Cui et al., 2013) showed both pathways **co-activate** during movement initiation. Current views see them as cooperative: the direct pathway promotes the selected action while the indirect pathway suppresses competitors, or the two encode different features of action such as vigor and value. Optogenetic stimulation of D1 MSNs promotes movement and of D2 MSNs suppresses it (Kravitz et al., 2010), supporting the classic polarity at the population level, but not strict segregation in time.

**Anatomical crosstalk.** Direct-pathway MSNs send collaterals to the GPe ("bridging collaterals"), and their number appears to change with dopamine levels, blurring pathway separation. The GPe also projects back to the striatum (arkypallidal neurons) and to the reticular thalamus.

**Patterns, not just rates.** In parkinsonism, the STN–GPe network develops synchronized bursting and exaggerated beta oscillations. High-frequency DBS seems to work less by silencing the target than by overriding pathological patterns with a regular signal, an "informational lesion," plus effects on passing axons and antidromic activation of cortex via the hyperdirect pathway. Optogenetic work in rodents suggested that driving cortical afferents to the STN can reproduce therapeutic effects (Gradinaru et al., 2009), though translation to humans remains an open question.

**Plasticity.** Corticostriatal synapses show dopamine-dependent long-term potentiation and depression with different rules in D1 and D2 MSNs. Chronic dopamine loss reshapes MSN dendritic spines (loss in D2 MSNs) and strengthens abnormal plasticity; pulsatile dopamine replacement may drive maladaptive plasticity underlying **levodopa-induced dyskinesia**.

The working model in 2020s research: a dynamical network with selection, learning and oscillatory components, of which the direct/indirect scheme is a useful first approximation.
levels.expert:
Clinicians still use the direct/indirect model daily because its predictions about targets mostly hold.

**Choosing a DBS target:**
- **STN**: strong effect on the cardinal motor signs and often allows a substantial reduction in dopaminergic medication, which can reduce dyskinesia indirectly. Small target; more potential for mood, cognitive and speech side effects in some patients.
- **GPi**: direct anti-dyskinetic effect, generally more flexible programming, medication usually not reduced as much. Often favored when there is significant cognitive or mood vulnerability or prominent dyskinesia. Large comparative trials found similar overall motor benefit, with differences in secondary outcomes.
- **VIM thalamus**: tremor only, not bradykinesia; used for essential tremor and selected tremor-dominant patients.

**Patient selection pearls:** the best single predictor of DBS motor benefit for Parkinson disease is a strong response to levodopa on a formal on/off challenge (tremor is an exception, since it can respond to DBS even when it responds poorly to medication). DBS does not help symptoms that don't respond to levodopa, such as freezing in the "on" state, falls from axial instability or dementia, and it does not slow the disease. Significant dementia is a relative contraindication.

**Hemiballismus**: usually from a small vascular lesion in or near the contralateral STN, often in older patients with diabetes or hypertension; nonketotic hyperglycemia can cause a similar picture with characteristic striatal changes on imaging. Most improve spontaneously over weeks; dopamine-blocking or depleting drugs help in the meantime.

**Postoperative pitfalls**: transient "microlesion" improvement right after lead placement (before stimulation is turned on) is common and should not be mistaken for final benefit. Sudden worsening years later should prompt a check of the device (battery depletion, lead fracture), because abrupt loss of stimulation can cause a severe akinetic crisis.

keyPoints: Direct pathway (D1, substance P): striatum inhibits GPi → thalamus disinhibited → more movement.
Indirect pathway (D2, enkephalin): striatum → GPe → STN released → GPi increased → less movement.
Hyperdirect pathway: cortex → STN, a fast brake.
Dopamine excites D1 direct MSNs and inhibits D2 indirect MSNs; both favor movement.
Hypokinetic disorders = too much GPi output; hyperkinetic = too little.
Real circuits show co-activation, crosstalk and oscillations beyond the simple model.

examples.tr: Stimulation disrupts the overactive, oscillating STN output that over-inhibits the thalamus.

lessons.title: Dopamine & the Nigrostriatal System

levels.kid:
Dopamine is a tiny messenger in your brain. It's like a "let's go!" signal.

Some special brain cells make dopamine. They live in a dark spot in the middle of your brain. They send long wires up to the movement helpers and squirt dopamine there.

With dopamine, moving is smooth and easy, like a bike with oiled wheels. Without enough, the wheels get rusty and moving gets slow and shaky.

Dopamine also helps you feel "yay, let's do that again!" when something good happens. That's how your brain learns what's worth doing.
levels.hs:
**Dopamine** is a neurotransmitter made from the amino acid tyrosine. The brain has several dopamine pathways:

- **Nigrostriatal**: from the substantia nigra pars compacta to the striatum. Controls movement. This is the pathway that fails in Parkinson disease.
- **Mesolimbic**: from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) to the nucleus accumbens. Involved in motivation and reward learning.
- **Mesocortical**: from the VTA to the prefrontal cortex. Involved in attention and planning.
- **Tuberoinfundibular**: from the hypothalamus to the pituitary stalk. Dopamine here keeps the hormone prolactin in check.

The nigrostriatal neurons contain a dark pigment called **neuromelanin**, which is why the substantia nigra looks black. In Parkinson disease, these neurons slowly die, and the area looks pale at autopsy. Symptoms usually appear only after a large share of them are already lost, because the brain compensates for years.

**How dopamine is made:** tyrosine → L-DOPA (by the enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase, the slow, rate-limiting step) → dopamine (by DOPA decarboxylase). It is broken down by the enzymes **MAO-B** and **COMT**.

Dopamine itself can't cross the blood–brain barrier, but L-DOPA can. That's why **levodopa** is the main treatment for Parkinson's. It's given with **carbidopa**, which stops levodopa from being converted to dopamine outside the brain.
levels.college:
**Synthesis and handling.** Tyrosine → L-DOPA (tyrosine hydroxylase, requires tetrahydrobiopterin, rate-limiting) → dopamine (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, AADC). Dopamine is packaged by **VMAT2** into vesicles, released, and cleared by the **dopamine transporter (DAT)**. Metabolism: MAO-B (glia) and COMT, producing homovanillic acid.

**Receptors.**
- D1-like (D1, D5): Gs/olf → adenylyl cyclase ↑ → cAMP ↑.
- D2-like (D2, D3, D4): Gi/o → cAMP ↓, K⁺ channel opening; D2 also serves as a presynaptic autoreceptor.

**Pharmacology of the nigrostriatal system (classes, no dosing):**
- **Levodopa + carbidopa**: precursor plus peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa doesn't cross the BBB, so it reduces peripheral side effects such as nausea).
- **Dopamine agonists** (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine): act directly on D2/D3 receptors; risk of impulse-control disorders, sleepiness and hallucinations.
- **MAO-B inhibitors** (selegiline, rasagiline, safinamide) and **COMT inhibitors** (entacapone, opicapone): prolong dopamine/levodopa action.
- **Amantadine**: NMDA antagonist used for levodopa-induced dyskinesia.

**Dopamine blockade** causes predictable problems: D2-blocking antipsychotics and some antiemetics (metoclopramide) can cause drug-induced parkinsonism, acute dystonia and, with long-term use, tardive dyskinesia. Blocking the tuberoinfundibular pathway raises prolactin.

**Imaging.** Dopamine transporter SPECT (ioflupane) shows reduced striatal uptake, starting in the posterior putamen, in Parkinson disease and other degenerative parkinsonisms, but is normal in essential tremor and drug-induced parkinsonism. It cannot reliably separate PD from atypical parkinsonisms like MSA or PSP.

**Toxic models.** MPTP is converted by MAO-B in glia to MPP⁺, which is taken up through DAT and poisons mitochondrial complex I in dopamine neurons, producing parkinsonism in humans and primates. 6-hydroxydopamine is used in rodent models.
levels.phd:
**Why are SNc neurons so vulnerable?** Several properties converge:

- **Huge axonal arbors**: each human SNc neuron is estimated to make an enormous number of striatal synapses (estimates run into the millions), with very long unmyelinated axons that demand vast energy.
- **Autonomous pacemaking** using Cav1.3 L-type calcium channels, which loads the cell with calcium and oxidant stress in mitochondria. This motivated a trial of the calcium channel blocker isradipine, which did not slow progression.
- **Dopamine chemistry**: cytosolic dopamine oxidizes to reactive quinones and neuromelanin; iron is abundant in the nigra.
- **Ventral tier selectivity**: ventrolateral SNc neurons projecting to the posterior putamen die first, matching the early posterior putaminal loss on DAT imaging.

**Alpha-synuclein.** Parkinson disease is defined pathologically by Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites rich in misfolded alpha-synuclein. Braak's staging (2003) proposed spread from the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and olfactory bulb up to the nigra and then the cortex, consistent with early non-motor symptoms (anosmia, constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder). Prion-like spread between cells is supported in models but debated in humans. A **seed amplification assay** detecting misfolded synuclein in CSF has emerged as a sensitive biomarker, and biological staging frameworks proposed in 2024 aim to define the disease by biology rather than symptoms; these frameworks are still being validated.

**Genetics.** Mutations in **SNCA**, **LRRK2**, **GBA1**, **PRKN**, **PINK1** and others account for a minority of cases; GBA1 variants are the most common genetic risk factor. PINK1 and parkin act in mitophagy, linking genetics to mitochondrial quality control.

**Dopamine and learning.** Phasic dopamine encodes reward prediction error; tonic dopamine may set vigor or the "cost of time." Dopamine replacement can therefore affect learning from outcomes, which helps explain impulse-control disorders on agonists, a striking example of circuit pharmacology.
levels.expert:
**Clinical management through a circuit lens (classes only, no dosing):**

**Early disease.** Levodopa is the most effective symptomatic drug. Fears that early levodopa accelerates the disease have not been supported by trials; motor complications relate more to disease duration and progressive loss of dopamine storage capacity. Agonists delay dyskinesia somewhat but carry higher risk of impulse-control disorders, sleep attacks and hallucinations, especially in older patients. Screen for compulsive gambling, shopping and eating at every visit when on agonists.

**Motor fluctuations.** As presynaptic terminals are lost, the striatum can't buffer levodopa, so the response tracks plasma levels: "wearing off," unpredictable "off" periods and peak-dose dyskinesia. Options: COMT or MAO-B inhibitors, extended-release formulations, continuous delivery by intestinal gel or subcutaneous infusion, and DBS.

**Must-know emergencies:**
- **Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome**: abrupt levodopa withdrawal (for example, a patient kept nil-by-mouth before surgery) can cause rigidity, fever and altered consciousness, resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Never stop dopaminergic medication abruptly in perioperative care; use alternative routes when needed.
- **Neuroleptic malignant syndrome** from D2 blockade: rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, high creatine kinase.
- **Avoid D2 blockers** (haloperidol, metoclopramide) in Parkinson patients; for psychosis, options with less D2 activity (such as quetiapine, clozapine) or pimavanserin are used.

**Imaging pearls.** Loss of the **swallow-tail sign** (nigrosome-1) on high-resolution susceptibility-weighted MRI supports a degenerative parkinsonism. Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI shows reduced signal in the SNc. DAT SPECT helps separate degenerative parkinsonism from essential tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism.

**Neurosurgical angle.** Restorative approaches have a long history: adrenal and fetal tissue grafts (mixed results, with graft-induced dyskinesia in some patients), gene therapies delivering AADC or growth factors, and recent early-phase trials of stem cell-derived dopamine neurons transplanted into the putamen. These are investigational.

lessons.title: Hypokinetic vs Hyperkinetic Disorders

levels.kid:
When the brain's go-and-stop team gets sick, two different things can happen.

Sometimes there is too much "stop." That's like Parkinson's disease. People move slowly, take tiny steps, feel stiff, and their hand might shake when it's resting in their lap.

Sometimes there is too little "stop." That's like Huntington's disease. Extra wiggly movements pop out that the person didn't plan, a bit like dancing they can't control.

Doctors have medicines that help, and brain surgeons can even put a tiny wire in the brain, like a pacemaker for the brain, to calm the signals down.
levels.hs:
Basal ganglia diseases fall into two big groups.

**Hypokinetic disorders** mean too little movement. The main example is **Parkinson disease**, caused by loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra. Its main signs (remember "TRAP"):

- **T**remor at rest (often "pill-rolling," fading with action)
- **R**igidity (stiffness, sometimes "cogwheel")
- **A**kinesia/bradykinesia (slowness and smaller movements)
- **P**ostural instability (balance problems, later in the disease)

Other clues: small handwriting, a quiet voice, a masked face and a shuffling walk. It's usually treated with **levodopa** and related drugs, and sometimes with **deep brain stimulation (DBS)**.

**Hyperkinetic disorders** mean too much movement. The main example is **Huntington disease**, a genetic disease caused by an expanded **CAG repeat** in the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4. It is **autosomal dominant**: each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting it. It causes **chorea** (brief, irregular, flowing movements), plus changes in thinking, mood and behavior. It damages the caudate nucleus first.

Other hyperkinetic movements include **hemiballismus** (wild flinging of one side, often from a small stroke in the subthalamic nucleus), **dystonia** (sustained twisting postures), **tics** and **tardive dyskinesia** (a side effect of long-term dopamine-blocking drugs).
levels.college:
**Parkinson disease (PD).** Bradykinesia plus rest tremor and/or rigidity defines parkinsonism; postural instability appears later. Onset is usually asymmetric. Non-motor features often precede motor signs: hyposmia, constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder, depression. Pathology: SNc neuron loss with Lewy bodies (alpha-synuclein).

**Red flags for atypical parkinsonism:** early falls, poor levodopa response, symmetry, rapid progression, early autonomic failure or dementia.
- **Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP)**: vertical gaze palsy (downgaze first), early backward falls, axial rigidity; tau pathology; midbrain atrophy ("hummingbird sign").
- **Multiple system atrophy (MSA)**: parkinsonism and/or cerebellar ataxia with early autonomic failure; glial synuclein inclusions; "hot cross bun" sign in the pons.
- **Dementia with Lewy bodies**: dementia before or within a year of parkinsonism, visual hallucinations, fluctuations, severe sensitivity to antipsychotics.
- **Corticobasal syndrome**: asymmetric rigidity, apraxia, alien limb.

**Huntington disease (HD).** Autosomal dominant CAG expansion in HTT. 40 or more repeats are fully penetrant; 36–39 reduced penetrance; 27–35 intermediate (not disease-causing but may expand in offspring). **Anticipation** (earlier onset in successive generations) is more marked with paternal transmission. Juvenile HD (often with large expansions) may present with rigidity rather than chorea. Early loss of indirect-pathway (D2/enkephalin) MSNs explains chorea; later loss of direct-pathway neurons leads to rigidity. Imaging: caudate atrophy with "boxcar" lateral ventricles. Chorea treatment: VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, valbenazine) or antipsychotics.

**Other causes of chorea:** Sydenham chorea (after group A strep, part of rheumatic fever), Wilson disease (copper; check in young patients with any movement disorder), drugs, autoimmune disease, pregnancy, and nonketotic hyperglycemia.

**Tardive dyskinesia**: repetitive orofacial movements after chronic D2 blockade; VMAT2 inhibitors are approved treatments.
levels.phd:
**Huntington disease mechanisms.** The polyglutamine-expanded huntingtin protein forms aggregates, but whether inclusions cause toxicity or are protective is debated. Proposed mechanisms include transcriptional dysregulation (for example, reduced BDNF support to the striatum from cortex), mitochondrial dysfunction and excitotoxicity via extrasynaptic NMDA receptors. A major insight from large genetic studies is that **somatic expansion** of the CAG repeat in vulnerable neurons, modified by DNA mismatch repair genes (such as MSH3 and FAN1), strongly influences age of onset. The number of **uninterrupted** CAG repeats predicts onset better than the total length in some families. These findings shifted therapy development toward slowing somatic expansion.

**Huntingtin-lowering therapies.** Antisense oligonucleotides lowering huntingtin were tested intrathecally; a large phase 3 trial of tominersen was halted in 2021 for lack of benefit, with possible signals in younger, less-affected participants. Gene therapy delivered directly into the striatum by neurosurgical infusion has since reported early encouraging results in a small trial (2025), which still needs confirmation. Allele-selective approaches and oral splicing modulators are also in development.

**Parkinson disease heterogeneity.** Subtypes (tremor-dominant vs postural instability/gait difficulty, or "brain-first" vs "body-first" synuclein spread) are proposed to explain different trajectories. The "body-first" hypothesis, with REM sleep behavior disorder and early autonomic signs, links to gut and peripheral synuclein pathology; it remains a hypothesis.

**Dystonia as a network disorder.** Dystonia involves the basal ganglia, cerebellum and sensorimotor cortex, with reduced surround inhibition and abnormal plasticity. Genetic dystonias (for example DYT-TOR1A) respond especially well to GPi DBS, often with gradual improvement over months, suggesting stimulation drives slow network plasticity rather than instantly blocking abnormal output.

**Tics and Tourette syndrome** implicate cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops; some patients receive DBS (often thalamic or GPi targets) in research or specialized centers.
levels.expert:
**Bedside approach to a movement disorder.** First decide: too little movement (hypokinetic) or too much (hyperkinetic)? Then name the movement precisely: tremor (rest, postural, kinetic), chorea, ballism, dystonia, myoclonus, tics. Then ask the key questions: age at onset, tempo (acute, subacute, chronic), family history, drug exposure (especially dopamine blockers), and whether the exam is otherwise focal.

**Acute or subacute hemichorea/hemiballism** in an adult: check glucose (nonketotic hyperglycemia), image for a stroke in the contralateral STN or striatum, and consider autoimmune or infectious causes. **Any movement disorder under about 50** should prompt testing for Wilson disease (ceruloplasmin, urinary copper, slit-lamp for Kayser–Fleischer rings), because it is treatable.

**Choosing surgery:**
- **Parkinson disease**: DBS of STN or GPi for motor fluctuations, dyskinesia or medication-refractory tremor in levodopa-responsive patients without significant dementia. Focused ultrasound lesioning (unilateral) is an option for tremor and selected cases.
- **Essential tremor**: VIM thalamic DBS or focused ultrasound thalamotomy (bilateral lesions carry higher risk of speech and balance problems, so staged treatment is used cautiously).
- **Dystonia**: GPi DBS, best results in primary generalized (especially TOR1A) dystonia; improvement may take months. Tardive dystonia also responds.
- **Huntington disease**: DBS for severe chorea has been reported but is not standard; the progressive cognitive and psychiatric decline dominates.

**Genetic testing ethics in HD**: predictive testing of an at-risk adult involves structured counseling. Testing of minors without symptoms is generally avoided so they can decide for themselves as adults. A confirmatory test in a symptomatic patient is different. Remember that testing one person can reveal a relative's status.

**Programming pearl:** Parkinson tremor and rigidity improve within seconds to minutes of stimulation; bradykinesia over minutes to hours; dystonia over weeks to months. Judge settings on the right timescale.

keyPoints: Hypokinetic disorders = too little movement (Parkinson disease); hyperkinetic = too much (chorea, ballism, dystonia).
Parkinson signs: rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability (TRAP).
Huntington disease: autosomal dominant CAG expansion in HTT (chromosome 4), caudate atrophy, chorea.
Early loss of indirect-pathway neurons explains chorea in Huntington disease.
Atypical parkinsonism red flags: early falls, poor levodopa response, early autonomic failure.
DBS targets: STN/GPi for PD, GPi for dystonia, VIM thalamus for essential tremor.
